qt: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI) Subject:

On 16 September 2026, the Commission President declared in her State of the Union address that ‘our Union is the strongest it has ever been’. At the same time, she spoke of a Europe that is securing its prosperity and breaking free from its dependence on Russian fossil fuels. Just nine days later, the Commissioner for Energy and Housing warned Member States that the EU was facing a ‘price crisis linked to a supply crisis’ and called on them to consider measures to reduce gas and electricity consumption ‘for as long as necessary’. At the same time, he also recommended lowering the temperature in public buildings and switching off street lighting. 1.

Does the Commission regard it as a sign of ‘the strongest Union in history’ when its Commissioner advises Member States to cut gas and electricity consumption, or did the Commission President simply fail to recognise the true state of the European energy sector in her speech?

Does the Commission regard it as a success of its energy policy that, after years of promises regarding energy security, diversification and ‘breaking free from dependence’, its solution to the price and supply crisis is, once again, to advise citizens and businesses to heat their homes less, use less lighting and consume less?

Is it perhaps the Commission’s aim that, following the introduction of ETS2 and further increases in the cost of emissions, energy will become so expensive that citizens will stop heating their homes and Member States will switch off their street lighting of their own accord, thereby resolving the problem of energy shortages?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2026) The EU has reduced its dependence on imported fossil fuels by 14.9% since 2022. The European Union has diversified away from Russian gas and has accelerated the development of domestic energy production through renewables. In 2026, the Commission has put forward AccelerateEU1 to progress even quicker, including through electrification of end-use sectors. The Commission’s recommendations on energy savings are part of the common EU response to high energy prices. Energy savings and energy efficiency are the first tools Europe can use to increase its energy resilience and independence in the short and long terms. The Commission continues to support Member States in addressing these challenges. In May 2026, it published a catalogue of national practices2 to help reduce gas and oil consumption, lower costs and deliver immediate savings for households, businesses and public authorities. Such measures improve resilience, reduce bills and cut emissions. The aim of the Emissions Trading System for buildings, road transport and additional sectors (ETS2) is to fight climate change. It will also play an important role in decoupling energy bills from high and volatile prices of imported fossil fuels. ETS2 will work together with complementary policies at EU and national level, providing a market incentive for investments in building renovations and clean mobility. ETS2 is designed for cost-efficiency, ensuring fossil fuel consumption is avoided or replaced first where clean alternatives costs are lowest. Revenues generated by ETS2 will be used to support decarbonisation and social measures. A part of ETS2 revenues finances the Social Climate Fund3 which specifically supports vulnerable groups in making clean investments, reducing their energy bills.
